Daily deep-dive · Day 1

Consistent Hashing

How distributed systems decide which server owns which data — without reshuffling everything every time a server joins or leaves.

01The problem, in plain words

Imagine you have millions of cache entries and 4 servers. You need a rule for "which server holds which key?" The obvious rule is hash(key) % 4 — divide by the number of servers, use the remainder.

It works perfectly… until server count changes. Go from 4 servers to 5, and hash(key) % 5 gives a different answer for almost every key. Nearly all your data is suddenly on the "wrong" server. Caches miss everywhere, databases get hammered, data has to migrate en masse.

Analogy: it's like assigning students to classrooms by "roll number ÷ number of rooms, take remainder." Open one new classroom and you've reassigned the whole school. What you really want: a new room takes a few nearby students, and everyone else stays put.

02The core idea

Put both keys and servers on the same circle (the hash output range bent into a ring, e.g. 0 to 2³²−1, wrapping around). Each key is owned by the first server you meet walking clockwise from the key's position.

The payoff: when a server leaves, only its keys slide to the next server clockwise. When a server joins, it takes over only a slice from one neighbor. On average just K/N keys move (K = keys, N = servers) — instead of nearly all of them.

03Key terminology

Hash ring (a.k.a. the continuum)
The full output range of a hash function treated as a circle — after the maximum value it wraps back to 0. Everything in this technique lives on this circle. Why it matters: a circle has no "end," so the rule "go clockwise to the next server" always finds an answer.
Node / server position
Each server is hashed (e.g. by its name or IP) to a point on the ring. That point marks where its territory begins. Why it matters: a server's position is stable — it doesn't depend on how many other servers exist. That's the whole trick.
Clockwise lookup (successor)
To find a key's owner: hash the key onto the ring, then walk clockwise until you hit a server. In code, this is a binary search over a sorted list of server positions. Why it matters: lookup is fast — O(log n) — and every client computes the same answer with no coordination.
Virtual nodes (vnodes / replicas)
Instead of one point per server, each server is hashed to many points (often 100–200), e.g. hash("serverA#1"), hash("serverA#2")… The server owns all the little arcs at those points. Why it matters: with one point per server, luck decides who gets a huge slice. Many small slices average out the load — and when a server dies, its load scatters across many neighbors instead of crushing one.
Rebalancing / key movement
The data migration that happens when membership changes. Consistent hashing's promise is that this is minimal: only keys in the affected arcs move. Why it matters: this is the metric the whole technique optimizes. Modulo hashing moves ~100% of keys; consistent hashing moves ~1/N of them.
Hot key / hotspot
A single extremely popular key (one celebrity's profile, one viral post). It hashes to exactly one place no matter what. Why it matters: consistent hashing balances how many keys each server gets, not how popular they are. Hotspots need other tools: replication, local caching, request coalescing.
Weighted placement
Giving a more powerful server more vnodes so it owns a bigger share of the ring. Why it matters: real clusters are rarely uniform hardware; vnode counts are the dial for that.

04What happens when a server dies

Before: ring has A, B, C. Key x sits just before B, so B owns it.
B disappears. Its positions vanish from the ring. Nothing else moves.
Lookups still work: walking clockwise from x now skips where B was and lands on the next server (say A). A is the new owner.
Only B's keys moved. Every key that belonged to A or C resolves exactly as before. With vnodes, B's keys spread across several servers, not just one.

05Where it's used

SystemHow it uses the idea
DynamoDB / CassandraPartition data across nodes; the ring (with vnodes) decides which node stores which partition.
Memcached (Ketama)Clients hash keys onto a ring of cache servers, so adding cache capacity doesn't invalidate everything.
CDNs & load balancersRoute the same user/content to the same backend ("sticky" routing) even as backends scale up and down. Envoy's ring-hash policy is exactly this.
Discord, chat systemsPin a channel/session to a particular server process so its state stays in one place.

06Common confusions

"Consistent" ≠ strong consistency. The name has nothing to do with consistency in the CAP-theorem sense. It means the key→server mapping stays mostly consistent when membership changes.
The ring is a concept, not a network. Servers aren't physically arranged in a circle and don't pass messages around one. The ring is just a sorted list of hash values that every client can compute independently.
It doesn't fix popularity imbalance. Equal key counts ≠ equal traffic. Hotspots remain a separate problem.

07One-sentence summary

Hash servers and keys onto the same circle, give each key to the next server clockwise — so when servers come and go, almost nothing has to move.
